items.title: Contains Duplicate
items.content:
A perfect first problem: three different solutions, three different complexities.

The problem

Return True if any value appears at least twice in nums, otherwise False.

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

Comparing every pair works but is O(n²). Can sorting help bring duplicates next to each other?

Hint 2

A set answers "have I seen this?" in O(1).

Solution 1: compare every pair, O(n²)

def has_dup_pairs(nums):
    return any(nums[i] == nums[j] for i in range(len(nums)) for j in range(i + 1, len(nums)))

print(has_dup_pairs([1, 2, 3, 1]))  # True

Solution 2: sort, then check neighbours, O(n log n)

def has_dup_sorted(nums):
    nums = sorted(nums)
    return any(nums[i] == nums[i - 1] for i in range(1, len(nums)))

print(has_dup_sorted([1, 2, 3, 4]))  # False

Solution 3: a set, O(n)

Like a bouncer with a guest list: if your name is already on it, you've been here before.

def contains_duplicate(nums):
    seen = set()
    for x in nums:
        if x in seen:
            return True
        seen.add(x)
    return False

print(contains_duplicate([1, 2, 3, 1]))  # True
print(contains_duplicate([1, 2, 3, 4]))  # False
print(contains_duplicate([]))            # False

A one-line version: len(set(nums)) != len(nums). It's neat, but the loop stops early as soon as it finds a duplicate.

Complexity

Mentioning this trade-off (time vs memory) is exactly what interviewers want to hear.

Walkthrough: the set solution step by step

Take nums = [4, 1, 7, 1] and follow the loop:

The loop stopped at the fourth item. On a list of a million numbers where the duplicate sits near the start, the loop version finishes almost instantly, while len(set(nums)) always builds the whole set first.

Common mistakes

  • Using a list instead of a set for seen. x in some_list scans the whole list, so the "fast" solution quietly becomes O(n²) again.
  • Sorting in place with nums.sort() when the caller still needs the original order. sorted(nums) makes a copy; mention which one you chose and why.
  • Forgetting the empty list. No values means no duplicates, so the answer is False. All three solutions above already handle it.

Follow-ups interviewers ask

  • *What if memory is very limited?* Use the sorting solution: it needs no extra set, at the cost of O(n log n) time.
  • *What if duplicates only count when they are at most k positions apart?* Keep a set of just the last k values, a sliding window. That is Contains Duplicate II.
  • *What if the numbers are in the range 1 to n?* You can mark visited values inside the list itself and use O(1) extra space.

Similar problems

Contains Duplicate II (within k positions), Valid Anagram, Single Number, Find the Duplicate Number.

Learn the pattern: Hashing.

items.title: Valid Anagram
items.content:
"listen" and "silent" use the same letters, just shuffled. That's an anagram.

The problem

Given strings s and t, return True if t is an anagram of s.

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

Two words are anagrams when every letter appears the same number of times in both.

Hint 2

Count letters with a dictionary. Or sort both words and compare.

Solution 1: sort both

def is_anagram_sorted(s, t):
    return sorted(s) == sorted(t)

print(is_anagram_sorted("listen", "silent"))  # True

O(n log n) because of sorting. Simple and perfectly fine to mention first.

Solution 2: count letters, O(n)

Imagine two bags of Scrabble tiles. Count each letter in the first bag, then remove letters for the second bag. If every count ends at zero, the bags match.

def is_anagram(s, t):
    if len(s) != len(t):
        return False
    count = {}
    for ch in s:
        count[ch] = count.get(ch, 0) + 1
    for ch in t:
        if count.get(ch, 0) == 0:
            return False
        count[ch] -= 1
    return True

print(is_anagram("anagram", "nagaram"))  # True
print(is_anagram("rat", "car"))          # False
print(is_anagram("ab", "a"))             # False

With Python's Counter it's one line:

from collections import Counter

print(Counter("anagram") == Counter("nagaram"))  # True

Complexity

  • Time O(n) for counting.
  • Space O(1) for lowercase English (at most 26 keys), O(k) for k different characters in general.

Walkthrough: counting "rat" vs "car"

Both words have three letters, so the length check passes. After counting s = "rat" the dictionary is {'r': 1, 'a': 1, 't': 1}. Now we walk through t = "car":

The very first letter of t is not in s at all, so we stop. For "anagram" and "nagaram" every letter finds a matching count, every count drops back to zero, and the function returns True.

Why check the length first?

If the lengths differ, the words can't be anagrams, and we skip all the counting. It also protects the second loop: without it, "ab" and "a" would pass because every letter of "a" is found in "ab", even though the extra "b" is never used.

Common mistakes

  • Comparing sets with set(s) == set(t). Sets forget how many times a letter appears, so "aab" and "abb" would wrongly look like anagrams.
  • Ignoring case and spaces when the question includes them. Ask first: is "Dormitory" an anagram of "dirty room"? If yes, lowercase both words and remove spaces before counting.
  • Assuming only a to z. With Unicode input (emojis, accented letters), a fixed array of 26 counts breaks, but a dictionary or Counter still works.

Follow-ups interviewers ask

  • *What if the inputs contain Unicode characters?* Use a dictionary instead of a 26-slot list.
  • *Can you do it with one dictionary pass?* Yes: add 1 for each letter of s and subtract 1 for each letter of t in the same loop, then check every count is zero.

Similar problems

Group Anagrams, Find All Anagrams in a String, Ransom Note, Permutation in String.

Learn the pattern: Hashing.

items.title: Group Anagrams
items.content:
The secret to many hash map problems is choosing the right key. Here the key is "the letters of the word, sorted".

The problem

Given a list of words, group the anagrams together. Any order of groups is fine.

Example

["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"] → [["eat", "tea", "ate"], ["tan", "nat"], ["bat"]]

Hints

Hint 1

All anagrams look identical once their letters are sorted: "eat", "tea" and "ate" all become "aet".

Hint 2

Use that sorted form as a dictionary key; the value is the list of words in the group.

Brute force

Compare every word with every group using an anagram check: O(n² · k). Too slow for big lists.

The easy idea: a label for every group

Think of sorting mail into pigeonholes. Each word gets a label (its sorted letters), and goes into the pigeonhole with that label.

Solution

from collections import defaultdict

def group_anagrams(words):
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for w in words:
        key = "".join(sorted(w))
        groups[key].append(w)
    return list(groups.values())

print(group_anagrams(["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"]))  # [['eat', 'tea', 'ate'], ['tan', 'nat'], ['bat']]
print(group_anagrams([""]))                                       # [['']]

Faster key: letter counts

Sorting each word is O(k log k). A tuple of 26 counts is O(k):

from collections import defaultdict

def group_anagrams_counts(words):
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for w in words:
        counts = [0] * 26
        for ch in w:
            counts[ord(ch) - ord("a")] += 1
        groups[tuple(counts)].append(w)       # lists can't be keys; tuples can
    return list(groups.values())

print(group_anagrams_counts(["abc", "bca", "xyz"]))  # [['abc', 'bca'], ['xyz']]

Complexity

  • Sorted key: O(n · k log k) time for n words of length k.
  • Count key: O(n · k) time.
  • Space O(n · k) to store the groups.

Walkthrough: building the groups

Follow the dictionary as each word arrives:

Every word is touched once, and the dictionary does the grouping for us. defaultdict(list) creates an empty list the first time a key appears, so we never need an if key not in groups check.

Common mistakes

  • Using a list as a key. sorted(w) returns a list, and lists can't be dictionary keys because they can change. Join it into a string or convert it to a tuple.
  • **Using set(w) as the key.** It loses repeated letters, so "aab" and "ab" would land in the same group.
  • Returning the dictionary itself instead of list(groups.values()). The question asks for a list of groups, not the labels.

Follow-ups interviewers ask

  • *Which key is better, sorted string or counts?* For short words the sorted string is simpler and fast enough. For long words the 26-count tuple wins because it avoids sorting.
  • *How would you return the groups sorted by size?* sorted(groups.values(), key=len, reverse=True).
  • *What if the input has uppercase letters?* Lowercase each word for the key, but store the original word in the group.

Similar problems

Valid Anagram, Group Shifted Strings, Find All Anagrams in a String.

Learn the pattern: Hashing.

items.title: Top K Frequent Elements
items.content:
"What are the top 10 trending hashtags?" is this exact problem.

The problem

Given nums and k, return the k most frequent values (any order).

Examples

Hints

Hint 1

Step one is always counting: a dictionary from value to count.

Hint 2

Sorting all counts is O(n log n). A heap of size k gives O(n log k).

Hint 3

Counts are between 1 and n. Could you use the count as a list index (buckets)?

Step 1: count

from collections import Counter

print(Counter([1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3]))  # Counter({1: 3, 2: 2, 3: 1})

Solution 1: sort by count, O(n log n)

from collections import Counter

def top_k_sort(nums, k):
    counts = Counter(nums)
    return sorted(counts, key=counts.get, reverse=True)[:k]

print(top_k_sort([1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], 2))  # [1, 2]

Solution 2: heap, O(n log k)

import heapq
from collections import Counter

def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
    counts = Counter(nums)
    return heapq.nlargest(k, counts, key=counts.get)

print(top_k_frequent([1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], 2))  # [1, 2]
print(top_k_frequent([4], 1))                 # [4]

Solution 3: bucket sort, O(n)

Make shelves numbered 1 to n. Put each value on the shelf matching its count. Then read shelves from the top down.

from collections import Counter

def top_k_buckets(nums, k):
    counts = Counter(nums)
    shelves = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]
    for value, c in counts.items():
        shelves[c].append(value)
    out = []
    for c in range(len(shelves) - 1, 0, -1):
        for value in shelves[c]:
            out.append(value)
            if len(out) == k:
                return out
    return out

print(top_k_buckets([1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], 2))        # [1, 2]
print(top_k_buckets([5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 7, 5, 5], 1))  # [5]

Complexity

Walkthrough: buckets for [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], k = 2

The counts are {1: 3, 2: 2, 3: 1}. We put each value on the shelf numbered by its count:

Reading from the top shelf down, we collect 1, then 2. That's k = 2 values, so we stop and return [1, 2]. A value can never appear more than n times, which is why n + 1 shelves are always enough.

Which solution should you write in an interview?

Start by saying the sort solution out loud: it's short and obviously correct. Then offer the heap, which is the answer most interviewers expect, and mention bucket sort as the O(n) option. heapq.nlargest keeps only k items in its heap, which matters when n is huge and k is small, such as the top 10 hashtags out of millions.

Common mistakes

  • Returning the counts instead of the values. The question wants [1, 2], not [3, 2].
  • **Using counts.most_common() without k.** It sorts everything; counts.most_common(k) is fine and uses a heap internally.
  • Off-by-one in the buckets. You need len(nums) + 1 shelves so that a value appearing n times has a shelf numbered n.

Follow-ups interviewers ask

  • *What if two values have the same count?* Ask which one should win. For "Top K Frequent Words", ties go to the alphabetically smaller word.
  • *What if the numbers arrive as an endless stream?* Keep running counts in a dictionary and a heap of size k, updating as each number arrives.

Similar problems

Top K Frequent Words, Kth Largest Element, Sort Characters by Frequency, K Closest Points to Origin.

Learn the pattern: Heaps.
